source_text: ΕΓΚΩΜΙΟΝ Εἰς τὸν ἅγιον μάρτυρα Ῥωμανὸν αʹ. αʹ. Πάλιν μαρτύρων μνήμη, καὶ πάλιν ἑορτὴ, καὶ, πανήγυρις πνευματική. Ἔκαμον ἐκεῖνοι, καὶ χαίρομεν ἡμεῖς· ἐπάλαισαν ἐκεῖνοι, καὶ ἡμεῖς ἀγαλλόμεθα· ἐκείνων ὁ στέφανος, καὶ κοινὸν τὸ κλέος, μᾶλλον δὲ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας ἁπάσης ἡ δόξα. Καὶ πῶς ἂν τοῦτο γένοιτο; φησίν. Ὅτι μέρη καὶ μέλη ἡμῶν εἰσιν οἱ μάρτυρες. Εἴτε δὲ πάσχει ἓν μέλος, συμπάσχει πάντα τὰ μέλη· εἴτε δοξάζεται ἓν μέλος, συγχαίρει πάντα τὰ μέλη. Ἡ κεφαλὴ στεφανοῦται, καὶ τὸ λοιπὸν σῶμα ἀγάλλεται· εἷς Ὀλυμπιονίκης γίνεται, καὶ ὁλόκληρος δῆμος εὐφραίνεται, καὶ μετὰ πολλῆς αὐτὸν δέχεται τῆς εὐφημίας. Εἰ δὲ ἐπὶ τῶν Ὀλυμπιακῶν ἀγώνων οἱ μηδὲν εἰς τοὺς ἱδρῶτας ἐκείνους εἰσενεγκόντες τοσαύτην καρποῦνται τὴν ἡδονὴν, πολλῷ μᾶλλον ἐπὶ τῶν τῆς εὐσεβείας ἀθλητῶν τοῦτο γένοιτ' ἄν. Πόδες ἐσμὲν ἡμεῖς, οἱ μάρτυρες κεφαλή· ἀλλ' οὐ δύναται εἰπεῖν ἡ κεφαλὴ τοῖς ποσὶ, Χρείαν ὑμῶν οὐκ ἔχω. Ἔνδοξα τὰ μέλη, ἀλλ' ἡ ὑπεροχὴ τῆς δόξης οὐ ποιεῖ τῆς πρὸ τὰ λοιπὰ μέρη συναφείας ἀλλοτρίωσιν· ταύτῃ γὰρ μάλιστα ἔνδοξα γίνεται, ὅταν τὴν πρὸς ἡμᾶς συνάφειαν μὴ διακρούσηται· ἐπεὶ καὶ ὀφθαλμὸς, τοῦ λοιποῦ παντὸς σώματος λαμπρότερος ὢν, τότε τὴν οἰκείαν διατηρεῖ δόξαν, ὅταν μὴ τοῦ λοιποῦ σώματος ἀποσχίζηται. Καὶ τί λέγω περὶ μαρτύρων; Εἰ γὰρ ὁ Δεσπότης αὐτῶν οὐκ ἐπῃσχύνθη γενέσθαι ἡμῶν κεφαλὴ, πολλῷ μᾶλλον αὐτοὶ μέλη ἡμῶν εἶναι οὐκ ἐπαισχύνονται· ἀγάπην γὰρ ἔχουσιν ἐῤῥιζωμένην, ἡ δὲ ἀγάπη τὰ διεστηκότα συνάπτειν καὶ συνδεῖν εἴωθε, καὶ περὶ τῆς ἀξίας οὐκ ἀκριβολογεῖται. Ὥσπερ οὖν αὐτοὶ συναλγοῦσιν ἡμῶν τοῖς ἁμαρτήμασιν, οὕτως ἡμεῖς συγχαίρομεν αὐτῶν τοῖς κατορθώμασιν. Οὕτω καὶ Παῦλος ἐκέλευσε ποιεῖν λέγων, Χαίρειν μετὰ χαιρόντων, καὶ κλαίειν μετὰ κλαιόντων. Ἀλλὰ τὸ μὲν κλαίειν μετὰ κλαιόντων εὔκολον, τὸ δὲ χαίρειν μετὰ χαιρόντων οὐ σφόδρα ῥᾴδιον· ῥᾷον γὰρ τοῖς ἐν συμφοραῖς οὖσι συναλγοῦμεν, ἢ τοῖς εὐδοκιμοῦσι συνηδόμεθα. Ἐκεῖ μὲν γὰρ αὐτὴ τῆς συμφορᾶς ἡ φύσις καὶ τὸν λίθον ἱκανὴ πρὸς συμπάθειαν ἐπικάμψαι· ἐνταῦθα δὲ ἐπὶ τῆς εὐπραγίας ὁ φθόνος καὶ ἡ βασκανία τὸν μὴ σφόδρα φιλοσοφοῦντα οὐκ ἀφίησι γενέσθαι κοινωνὸν τῆς ἡδονῆς. Ὥσπερ γὰρ ἡ ἀγάπη τὰ διῃρημένα συνάγει καὶ συνδεῖ, οὕτως ἡ βασκανία τὰ ἡνωμένα διαιρεῖ. Διὸ παρακαλῶ, μελετήσωμεν συγχαίρειν τοῖς εὐδοκιμοῦσιν, ἵνα καὶ φθόνου καὶ βασκανίας τὴν ψυχὴν ἐκκαθάρωμεν· οὐδὲν γὰρ οὕτως ἀπελαύνει τὸ νόσημα τοῦτο τὸ χαλεπὸν καὶ δυσίατον, ὡς τὸ συνήδεσθαι τοῖς ἐν ἀρετῇ βιοῦσιν. Ἄκουσον γοῦν πῶς ὁ Παῦλος ἐν ἑκατέροις τούτοις ἐστὶν ἄκρος· Τίς, φησὶν, ἀσθενεῖ, καὶ οὐκ ἀσθενῶ; τίς σκανδαλίζεται, καὶ οὐκ ἐγὼ πυροῦμαι; Οὐκ εἶπε, καὶ οὐκ ἐγὼ λυποῦμαι, ἀλλ', οὐκ ἐγὼ πυροῦμαι, τῇ προσηγορίᾳ, τῆς πυρώσεως τὴν ἐπίτασιν τῆς ὀδύνης ἡμῖν παραστῆσαι βουλόμενος. Καὶ πάλιν ἑτέροις γράφων, Χωρὶς ἡμῶν ἐβασιλεύσατε, φησίν· καὶ ὄφελόν γε ἐβασιλεύσατε, ἵνα καὶ ἡμεῖς ὑμῖν συμβασιλεύσωμεν· καὶ πάλιν· Νῦν ζῶμεν, ἐὰν ὑμεῖς στήκητε ἐν Κυρίῳ. Ὅρα πῶς περισπούδαστος ἦν αὐτῷ τῶν ἀδελφῶν ἡ εὐδοκίμησις, ὃς οὔτε ζῇν ἐνόμιζεν, ἐκείνων μὴ σωζομένων.
thought_title: Martyrs as head, Church as body: shared joy
orientation: Chrysostom opens his encomium for the martyr Romanus by explaining why the Church celebrates the martyrs' victory as its own.
pass_a_gloss: Encomium on the holy martyr Romanus, discourse 1. Again a memory of martyrs, and again a feast, and a spiritual assembly. Those ones labored, and we rejoice; those ones wrestled, and we exult; theirs is the crown, and common is the glory, or rather the glory of the whole Church. And how would this happen? he says. Because parts and members of us are the martyrs. And if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; if one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with it. The head is crowned, and the rest of the body exults; one Olympic victor comes into being, and a whole people rejoices, and with much acclaim receives him. But if in the Olympic contests those who contributed nothing to those labors reap so much pleasure, much more in the case of the athletes of piety would this happen. Feet are we, the martyrs are head; but the head cannot say to the feet, I have no need of you. Glorious are the members, but the preeminence of glory does not produce estrangement from the connection to the remaining parts; for by this especially they become glorious, when they do not reject the connection to us; since also the eye, being more splendid than all the rest of the body, then preserves its own glory, when it is not cut off from the rest of the body. And why do I speak about martyrs? For if their Master was not ashamed to become our head, much more are they not ashamed to be members of us; for they have love rooted, and love is accustomed to join and bind together things that stand apart, and does not quibble about worth. Just as therefore they grieve with us over our sins, so we rejoice with them over their successes. Thus also Paul commanded us to do, saying, Rejoice with those who rejoice, and weep with those who weep. But weeping with those who weep is easy, while rejoicing with those who rejoice is not very easy; for more easily do we grieve with those who are in misfortunes than we rejoice with those who are prospering. For there the very nature of the misfortune is sufficient to bend even a stone toward sympathy; but here in the case of prosperity envy and malice do not allow the one who is not very philosophical to become a sharer of the pleasure. For just as love gathers and binds together things that are divided, so malice divides things that are united. Therefore I exhort, let us practice rejoicing with those who prosper, so that we may purge the soul of both envy and malice; for nothing so drives away this disease, which is grievous and hard to cure, as rejoicing with those who live in virtue. Hear then how Paul is supreme in both of these: Who, he says, is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not on fire? He did not say, and I am not grieved, but, and I am not on fire, wishing by the term of burning to present to us the intensity of the pain. And again writing to others, Without us you reigned, he says; and would that indeed you reigned, so that we also might reign with you; and again: Now we live, if you stand firm in the Lord. See how precious to him was the good repute of the brothers, who did not even consider himself to be living, if those ones were not being saved.

choices.why: The glossary bans 'gathering' for Ἐκκλησία but not for πανήγυρις; 'assembly' preserves the festal, corporate sense of πανήγυρις while 'spiritual' marks it as non-earthly.

choices.english: Those ones labored, and we rejoice
choices.why: The parallel aorist/present contrast (their past labor, our present joy) is kept exactly; 'those ones' preserves the demonstrative force of ἐκεῖνοι.
rejected: They toiled, and we are glad

choices.why: The term is a specific compound for a winner at the Olympic games; 'victor' keeps the athletic register without importing 'champion' connotations.
ἀθλητής is the standard term for a contestant in games, and Chrysostom is extending the athletic metaphor to the martyrs; 'athletes' preserves the metaphor.
ἀκριβολογέομαι means to be precise or exacting about something; 'quibble about worth' captures the sense that love does not make fine distinctions about rank or dignity.
rejected: does not split hairs over rank

choices.why: The verb πυρόω literally means 'to burn' or 'to be set on fire'; Chrysostom explicitly comments on this term as conveying intensity of pain, so a literal rendering is required.

pass_b_english: Again the memory of the martyrs, again a feast, and a spiritual assembly. Those ones labored, and we rejoice; those ones wrestled, and we exult. The crown is theirs, and the glory is shared—or rather, the glory belongs to the whole Church. And how can this be, someone says? Because the martyrs are our parts and members. If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; if one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it (1 Corinthians 12:26). The head is crowned, and the rest of the body exults. One Olympic victor emerges, and a whole people rejoices and receives him with great acclaim. If in the Olympic games those who contributed nothing to those labors enjoy such great pleasure, how much more would this happen with the athletes of piety? We are the feet, the martyrs are the head. But the head cannot say to the feet, “I have no need of you” (1 Corinthians 12:21). The members are glorious, but the surpassing glory does not make them strangers to their connection with the remaining parts. For they become glorious especially when they do not break off their connection with us. Even the eye, though brighter than all the rest of the body, preserves its own glory precisely when it is not cut off from the rest of the body. And why do I speak about martyrs? If their Master was not ashamed to become our head, much more are they not ashamed to be our members. For they have love rooted within them, and love is accustomed to join and bind together things that stand apart, and it does not quibble about worth. Just as they suffer with us in our sins, so we rejoice with them in their achievements. Paul commanded us to do this when he said, “Rejoice with those who rejoice, and weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15). But weeping with those who weep is easy, while rejoicing with those who rejoice is not very easy. For we more readily suffer with those in misfortune than we share joy with those who prosper. In the one case, the very nature of misfortune is enough to bend even a stone toward sympathy; but in the other case, with prosperity, envy and malice do not allow anyone who is not deeply philosophical to become a partner in the pleasure. For just as love gathers and binds together what is divided, so malice divides what is united. Therefore I urge you, let us practice rejoicing with those who prosper, so that we may cleanse our souls of envy and malice. For nothing drives away this harsh and hard-to-cure disease as much as sharing joy with those who live in virtue. Listen, then, to how Paul excels in both of these. “Who is weak,” he says, “and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not on fire?” (2 Corinthians 11:29). He did not say, “and I am not grieved,” but “and I am not on fire,” wanting to show us by this term the intensity of the pain. And again, writing to others, he says, “You have begun to reign without us—and I wish you had begun to reign, so that we also might reign with you” (1 Corinthians 4:8). And again: “Now we live, if you stand firm in the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 3:8). See how precious the good reputation of his brothers was to him—he did not even consider himself alive if they were not being saved.
